title: Food banks
hookLine: ordinary church halls feeding neighbors every week

lines: TUESDAY, FOUR O'CLOCK, A CHURCH HALL.
TINS, BREAD, A LIST OF NAMES.
cards: Tuesday, four in the afternoon, a church hall that smells of floor polish and instant coffee. Folding tables in a row. Tins of beans, pasta, peanut butter, a crate of bread a bakery dropped off this morning.

A retired teacher checks names on a list, kindly, without fuss. A teenager carries bags out to a car. A man in a work jacket studies the floor while he waits, until someone asks about his kids, and he looks up.
None of this will reach a history book. And next Tuesday the tables go up again.

teach.b: In Mark a crowd has followed Jesus to a lonely place, and it's getting late. The disciples suggest the sensible thing: send them away to buy bread in the villages.
Jesus answers, in the King James words: "Give ye them to eat." Not, leave it to me. You.
The disciples protest that they can't afford it.

teach.h: FIVE LOAVES: START WITH WHAT YOU HAVE.
teach.b: He asks what they have. "Five, and two fishes." The story ends with everyone fed and "twelve baskets full of the fragments" left over.
Christians read that miracle in more than one way, but the order is plain: the hungry are handed to the disciples, and what they already have is where it starts.
Then Matthew 25, a verse before the line the hospice lesson used.
The king says: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." The people are puzzled. When?
He answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Read that way, the man in the work jacket is not a project.
In the story's terms, Christ is standing in the line. That changes the posture: a chair, a name, a question about his kids. Not every food bank is run by a church, and churches run them differently.
Some hand out bags. Some set up a small shop where people choose. Some cook a hot meal and eat with their guests.
Some Christians ask why the line is there at all: wages, rent, illness.
Others say: feed today, argue tomorrow. Both are reading the same Gospels.

how: Church congregations host or support food banks and community meals, collecting food at services, staffing distribution days with volunteers, and pointing to Jesus's words in Mark 6 and Matthew 25.

o: places where neighbors hand out food to people in need
storehouses that keep a town's grain for the winter
shops that sell groceries cheaply to their members

games.q: the hall and the Gospels — tap the pairs.

s: in Mark, Jesus tells the disciples to send the crowd away to buy food
sending them away was the disciples' idea. Jesus said: "give ye them to eat."
in Matthew 25, the king says he himself was hungry
"for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." what was done for the least of these was done for him.
every food bank is run by a church
not every one is, and churches that run them do it in different ways: bags, small shops, hot meals.

games.q: you're a disciple. it's late, the place is lonely, and a huge crowd is hungry. you have five loaves and two fish. what does Jesus tell you?
o: send them home to buy bread in the villages.
feed only the ones who came first.
games.why: Mark 6:37. the disciples wanted to send the crowd away. Jesus handed the problem back to them, and started with what they had.

practice: Open your kitchen cupboard in your mind and find something you'd be glad to eat yourself: not the dented tin from the back, but something good. Then picture the hall, the folding table, the line, one face.
If you pray, you can pray for whoever will open that bag; if you don't, just hold them in mind kindly.

wordCard.voice: Food banks. Church halls and other places where neighbors bring food and hand it to neighbors, week after week, behind them the command in Mark: give ye them to eat.

orig.note: Greek: give ye them to eat (Mark 6:37). the Greek spells out the 'you' as well.

carryVoice: Your line: give them to eat. Start with what you have. Day nine hundred ninety-eight, done.
